newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak amendment seen curbing central bank powers.
newsitem.headline: Slovak amendment seen curbing central bank powers.

text.p: A controversial amendment to the Slovak securities law passed this week may significantly weaken central bank powers to regulate the ownership of domestic banks, analysts said on Friday.

According to the current banking law any private entity needs National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) approval to buy more than a 15 percent stake in a bank. It also stipulates bank shares must be registered at the official securities registry.

But on Tuesday parliament approved the amendment which effectively gives majority shareholders the right to change the status of stock it holds to bearer shares where the owner's name remains unregistered.

This, together with the fact that the amendment also reintroduces over-the-counter trading without registration on the main markets, may lead to a complete anonymity of any buyer into a company or bank, the analysts said.
The NBS has been embroiled in a dispute with steel maker VSZ a.s. over its ambitions to take a large stake in IRB Bank.
In a case exemplifying the lack of transparency of the Slovak equities market, VSZ appears to have taken more than 15 percent of IRB without NBS approval.

It later transpired that VSZ's stake had fallen slightly below the 15 percent level but the NBS then ruled that it was acting in concert with a broker based in the steelmaker's home city of Kosice to take more than the permitted level.
The broker later said it had sold its stake but has appealed against the NBS order.
Analysts and brokers said what mattered was not so much the status of the shares of the bank, but whether the stock of the company buying into it was in the form of bearer shares.

"If we take VSZ and IRB as an example, according to the amendment there seems to be no measure to reveal the real VSZ holding in the bank," said Dusan Sykora, a broker at ING Barings. "The firm could create a company with unregistered shares, which on its behalf will buy stakes in the bank."

In October, VSZ announced it was interested in increasing its stake in IRB to as much as 40 percent. But the NBS rejected the VSZ request because it had not presented its plan on participation in restructuring of the bank.
Shortly after the central bank ruling, VSZ President Jan Smerek said "there are other ways of getting the 40 percent".
NBS Governor Vladimir Masar said on Thursday it would be premature to predict all possible effects of the amendment on its power to control ownership of banks.

But he said the NBS was likely to have to revise its legal powers. He also admitted that the central bank already found it difficult to control the consequences of several entities acting in concert to buy into a bank.

Analysts and brokers said the amended law effectively opens the way for a potential buyer of a bank to bypass the 15 percent limit, as it permits owners of a company to mask holdings behind unregistered stock.

"If the law in fact allows trading shares outside the scrutiny of the market to an anonymous entity, it could lead to sales to completely unknown buyers, for example even to the Russian mafia," said Martin Barto, an ING Barings analyst.
